chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A compass keeps one distance fixed, so circles and arcs give exact lengths; squares and rectangles are then built from their properties, and the same two ideas, perpendiculars and arcs, find every corner.

points.title: Draw, then reason
points.text: Each construction starts from a rough diagram and a prediction, then the steps are carried out and checked with a ruler and a protractor.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, one tool to do it by hand where the manipulation is the idea, then the book's construction questions in a practice topic.

points.title: Properties do the work
points.text: A square and a rectangle have fixed properties, so we measure only what is needed and the properties give the remaining sides and angles.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: Wrong ideas such as 'a square is not a rectangle' or 'a diagonal always splits a corner into two equal angles' are raised by Keeko and fixed with a drawing, never just a rule.

Worked example: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
1. Look at each picture and spot the circles in it.
2. Sketch the circles in the right places and sizes.
3. Compare your freehand circles with the pictures and see how round they are.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.

3. This curve is a circle with centre P.
Answer: They would form a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

concepts.concept_name: The compass draws the circle: centre and radius

content.text:
You can start by marking a few points of distance 4 cm from P using the compass. How can this be done?
You will have to open up the compass against a ruler (see Fig. 8.2) such that the distance between the tip of the compass and the pencil is 4 cm.
Now, try to get the full curve.
Hint: Keep the point of the compass fixed moving only the pencil.
What is the shape of the curve? It is a circle!
Take a point on the circle. What will be its distance from P, equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? Similarly, what will be the distance between P and another point on the circle?
As shown in the figure, the point P is called the centre of the circle and the distance between the centre and any point on the circle is called the radius of the circle.

content.text:
Worked example: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
1. Place the compass next to a ruler and open it until the tip and the pencil point are 4 cm apart.
2. Put the tip firmly on P.
3. Keep the tip fixed and move only the pencil all the way round.
Answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.

concepts.concept_name: The compass draws the circle: centre and radius

content.text:
Worked example: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?
1. The pencil stayed exactly 4 cm from the tip all the time.
2. So every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
3. This fixed distance is the radius; P is the centre.
Answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.

content.text:
Activity (section 8.1): Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.
1. Choose a radius and set the compass with the ruler.
2. Fix the tip at each centre and draw each circle.
3. For concentric circles, keep the same tip point and change the radius.
4. Add the dots and lines with a ruler.
Answer: Open ended. Correct drawings: touching circles have centres at a distance of twice the radius; concentric circles share one centre but have different radii; overlapping circles have centres closer than twice the radius; the mouse face has all its circles drawn with a compass.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?
1. Draw the head circle with the compass.
2. Draw the neck as a short vertical line below the circle.
3. Draw the body as a rectangle without the top edge: two vertical sides and a flat bottom.
4. Fix a radius and try the tip at different spots above the body until the arc from one top corner to the other touches the bottom of the neck line.
5. Draw the arc and rub out the trial marks.
Answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an eye is two curves meeting at two pointed ends. Do both curves use the same radius?
2. Draw two light guide lines. The tip of the upper curve is on one line and the tip of the lower curve is on the other.
3. Keep the same radius and the same distance from the middle for both tips. Then the eye is symmetrical, and the second eye is a copy of the first.

content.text:
Worked example: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
1. Draw two light horizontal guide lines (supporting lines) that help to place the compass tips.
2. Choose a radius and place the tip at B to draw the upper curve between the two corners.
3. Place the tip at A, the same distance from the middle on the other side, and with the same radius draw the lower curve.
4. Fill the pupil circle in the middle.
5. Repeat for the second eye and adjust until both eyes are symmetrical and identical.
Answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points A and B) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.

concepts.concept_name: The two properties of a rectangle and of a square

content.text:
Now, let us look at some basic figures having straight lines in their boundary.
What shapes are these? Yes, these are our familiar squares and rectangles. But what makes them squares and rectangles?
Consider this rectangle ABCD.
The points A, B, C and D are the corners of the rectangle. Lines AB, BC, CD and DA are its sides. Its angles are ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D.
The blue sides AB and CD are called opposite sides, as they lie opposite to each other. Likewise, AD and BC is the other pair of opposite sides.
Recall that, in a rectangle:
R1) The opposite sides are equal in length, and
R2) All the angles are 90°.
As in the case of rectangles, the corners and sides are defined for a square in the same manner.
A square satisfies the following two properties:
S1) All the sides are equal, and
S2) All the angles are 90°.

4. D has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.

concepts.concept_name: A rotated square is still a square

content.text:
Here is a square piece of paper having all its sides equal in length and all angles equal to 90°. It is rotated as shown in the figure. Is it still a square?
Let us check if the rotated paper still satisfies the properties of a square.
Are all the sides still equal? Yes.
Are all the angles still 90°? Yes.
Rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles.
Therefore, this rotated figure satisfies both the properties of a square and so, it is a square.
By the same reasoning, a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.2)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.2): Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.
1. Draw the rectangle on dots, counting dots along each side.
2. From each corner of the rectangle, move one dot diagonally outwards (same count each time).
3. Draw an equal square at each of the four places, counting the same number of dots for every square.
4. Use the same counts on the left and right, top and bottom so the figure is symmetrical.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (section 8.2)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 8.2): Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
1. Pick dots as corners so that each side goes the same number of dots across and down for a square.
2. Join the corners with a ruler.
3. Measure the sides with the ruler.
4. Check the angles with a protractor or a set square.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and 4 angles of 90°. For example a diamond with corners 4 dots up, 4 dots right, 4 dots down and 4 dots left of its centre is a square.
